task:
Let Lark parse or lex part of a larger string without copying it, and with token positions that refer to the whole string. Today the only way is to slice the string, which loses the real positions and the context for regex lookbehind.

Add a class TextSlice, importable as lark.TextSlice and from lark.utils. It is a frozen dataclass with fields text, start and end.

- text must be a str or bytes. Anything else raises TypeError.
- A negative start or end counts from the end of text, as in Python slicing. end may be None, meaning the end of text.
- TextSlice.cast_from(x) returns x if it is already a TextSlice, and otherwise TextSlice(x, 0, len(x)).
- len() of a slice is end - start. is_complete_text() is true when the slice covers all of text. count(sub) and rindex(sub) work within the slice.

Lark.parse, Lark.lex and Lark.parse_interactive accept a TextSlice wherever they accept a string.

- Only the text between start and end is lexed. Like Python's re with pos and endpos, a regex can look behind start but sees nothing past end. With %ignore /\s+/ and terminals WORD: /\b\w+\b/, FRAG_END: /\B\w+/ and FRAG_START: /\w+\B/, parsing TextSlice(" abc def ", 1, -1) gives WORD abc and WORD def, and so does TextSlice(" abc def ", -8, 8). TextSlice("xabc def ", 1, -1) gives FRAG_END abc and WORD def. TextSlice(" abc defx", 1, -1) gives WORD abc and WORD def.
- Token positions refer to the whole text. For the text "1\n2\n3\n...\n9" and a grammar of newlines and single characters, parsing TextSlice(text, 2, 3) gives one token "2" with start_pos 2 and line 2. TextSlice(text, -1, None) gives "9" with start_pos 16 and line 9.
- lex works the same way: for a basic-lexer grammar of "a" "b" "c" "d" with %ignore " ", lexing TextSlice("xxxabc cba ddxx", 3, -2) gives the tokens a b c c b a d d.

This must work with the LALR parser and with Earley on the basic lexer. Lexers that cannot honour a slice must raise TypeError when given one that does not cover the whole text: the Earley dynamic and dynamic_complete lexers, and old-style custom lexers.

Custom lexers declare their interface with the class attribute __future_interface__, now an integer. 0, or a missing attribute, is the old interface: lex(text) gets a plain string. 1, which True also means, is the current interface: lex(lexer_state, parser_state). 2 is the new interface, where lexer_state.text is a TextSlice, so such a lexer can pass the state on to a built-in lexer unchanged. Any other value raises ValueError. Interfaces 0 and 1 raise TypeError for a partial slice.

Everything else must keep working, including the standalone parser generator.
